title: Figures
text: Each figure below is the plate as it appears in the manuscript. The claim is stated in a sentence or two; the statistics behind it, and the caveats that go with them, live in the paper rather than here.

title: Figures
section: Figure 1: Characterization of the three CD8 reference atlases
text:
Figure 1: Characterization of the three CD8 reference atlases
What the three CD8 reference atlases are, before any query cohort is annotated.


The three reference atlases used throughout differ in what they contain, where their cells came from, and how they were built, before a single query cell is labelled. Everything that follows is downstream of these differences rather than of the annotation software.

title: Figures
section: Figure 2: Tpex definitions and their expression profiles across atlases
text:
Figure 2: Tpex definitions and their expression profiles across atlases
What each reference atlas calls Tpex, and what those cells express.

Each atlas names a progenitor-exhausted population, and each defines it by a different expression programme. The labels are not three names for one population, and the figure shows where each sits on two published exhaustion rulers.

title: Figures
section: Figure 3: Clonal adjudication of the two huARdb Tpex poles
text:
Figure 3: Clonal adjudication of the two huARdb Tpex poles
huARdb’s two Tpex poles judged clonally, where the receptor and the transcriptome disagree about which one is the progenitor.

One reference names two progenitor poles of its own. Judged by T-cell receptor sharing rather than by expression, the pole that looks most stem-like transcriptionally is the one least connected to the expanded exhausted lineage.

title: Figures
section: Figure 4: Shared progenitor core and divergence between reference Tpex definitions
text:
Figure 4: Shared progenitor core and divergence between reference Tpex definitions
The references share a small progenitor core, diverge beyond it, and pair across atlases rather than within one.

A narrow set of progenitor genes is common to all three references. Past that core the definitions separate, and the labels that most resemble one another sit in different atlases rather than in the same one.

title: Figures
section: Figure 5: Recovery of author-defined Tpex by each reference atlas
text:
Figure 5: Recovery of author-defined Tpex by each reference atlas
Reference atlases place their Tpex label on cells the query authors called something else, and the four definitions differ from each other in programme, in composition and in continuum position.

When a reference annotates a published cohort, its Tpex call frequently lands on cells the original authors assigned to a different state. The four progenitor definitions then differ from one another on every axis measured here.

title: Figures
section: Figure 6: Reference versus algorithm contribution to the Tpex call, and label reproducibility
text:
Figure 6: Reference versus algorithm contribution to the Tpex call, and label reproducibility
The reference atlas decides which cells are called Tpex, and whether the label is reproducible at all.

Holding the reference fixed and changing the annotation algorithm preserves most of the Tpex call; holding the algorithm fixed and changing the reference does not, in every cohort tested. For one of the three references the progenitor label is the least reproducible label between patients that its own vocabulary names, and it is near-worst in a second.

title: Figures
section: Figure 7: Compositional and clinical consequences of the annotation choice
text:
Figure 7: Compositional and clinical consequences of the annotation choice
Swapping the annotation loses a published clinical result.

Five views of one cohort, narrowing from the whole composition to a single label and ending on survival. Whole-composition separation by pathological response is weak but real, and its size depends on which reference is adopted. The variance driving it sits in different cell types under each reference: two of the three place their own progenitor label among the features carrying it, while huARdb places both of its poles near the bottom. Tested state by state, and again across huARdb’s published hierarchy, no progenitor label carries the response signal. A published biomarker built from clonal structure reproduces on its own construction, but no reference’s transcriptomic Tpex label reconstitutes it.

title: Tpex Data Portal
text: An overview of the study behind the figures. Findings are preliminary. Human tumors carry no ground-truth Tpex label, so every claim below concerns where each reference draws the boundary, not which tool is correct.

title: Tpex Data Portal
text:
The question
Automated annotation tools disagree about which CD8 T cells are progenitor-exhausted (Tpex). This study asks whether that disagreement originates in the annotation algorithm or in the reference atlas’s definition of Tpex, and what difference the answer makes to a clinical conclusion.
Tpex is not confined to tumor. It is reported across lymphoid tissue, including draining lymph nodes, spleen and tertiary lymphoid structures. The cells annotated here are CD8 T cells from tumor, and from paired lymph node where a cohort provides it.
Three references each name an explicit progenitor state. huARdb names two of its own, giving four in total:








Reference
Progenitor label
Notes




CD8 TILs
CD8.TPEX
built entirely from tumor and metastasis TILs


Chu pan-cancer
CD8_c7_p-Tex



huARdb v2
Tpex
the narrow SELL+ pole


huARdb v2
Tex-Tpex
the union of its two deposited IL7R+ exhausted labels

title: Tpex Data Portal
text:
How the pipeline works
One pipeline is applied identically to every cohort, so the only quantity varying inside the factorial is the (algorithm, reference) pair.

Ingest and harmonise: each study’s counts are rebuilt into a standard object with harmonised metadata, and single-cell TCR is joined where available.
Quality control: run through nf-core/scdownstream, and characterised per cohort rather than used to drop cells. The original authors’ QC was sound throughout, so no cohort is filtered more aggressively than another. Doublet and ambient-RNA sensitivity analyses leave the headline unchanged.
Purify to CD8 TILs: scGate CD8_TIL gating per sample, so every tool sees the same universe of cells.
Run the factorial: six algorithms (ProjecTILs, Symphony, Seurat anchor transfer, scPoli, scAtlasVAE, PopV) crossed with three references, giving 16 usable pipelines once structurally impossible combinations are dropped.
Adjudicate: against clonal lineage, marker phenotype and run-to-run reproducibility, none of which depends on a further annotation.

Analysis runs on 8 held-out cohorts and 704,304 CD8 T cells. Held-out means the cohort appears in no reference’s training data. Pan-cancer atlases share source studies with published query cohorts, so overlapping pairs are reported separately as self-consistency checks and never as headline numbers.

title: Tpex Data Portal
text:
What we find

The reference changes the Tpex call more than the algorithm does
Agreement between two annotations of the same cells is measured with the overlap coefficient (Szymkiewicz–Simpson), the intersection over the smaller set. Holding the reference fixed and swapping the algorithm retains most of the Tpex call. Holding the algorithm fixed and swapping the reference retains little of it, and the reference swap costs the greater agreement in all eight cohorts. Figure 6 carries the values, and the agreement explorer recomputes them for every state and every cohort.
The claim is comparative. Algorithm-swap agreement is itself well below 1, so the algorithm also changes the call. Jaccard is not used: it divides by the union and is bounded by 1/r when two sets differ in size by a factor r, which would inflate this contrast several-fold.
The other states behave differently, and not uniformly. Terminal exhaustion is recovered across pipelines: agreement stays high whichever of the two choices is swapped. Naive is nearly as stable, with a small tail of pairs that disagree sharply. Tpex is the least stable state and central memory the second least, so reference dependence is not unique to the progenitor label, though it is most severe there.


Two of three references cannot reproduce their own progenitor label
Inter-sample consistency (scTypeEval) asks whether a label is reproducible between patients inside its own vocabulary, so it never compares across references. ProjecTILs’ CD8.TPEX is the worst-posed label its own reference names, in a vocabulary that is otherwise the most reproducible of the three. huARdb’s Tex-Tpex is near-worst in its own. Chu’s p-Tex is the exception on one axis, its global consistency placing its joint rank at 12 of 13. Roughly half of all labels sit below the method’s local guide line, so that line is not a pass/fail threshold and is not read as one here.
huARdb’s narrow Tpex clears the metric’s minimum-sample gate in 0 of 42 arms, so in none of the eight cohorts can its consistency be evaluated. That reflects scorability rather than a low score.


Whether patients separate at all depends on the reference
Before asking about any single label, ask whether the annotation changes how patients stratify. Per-patient compositions are centred-log-ratio transformed and tested with ANOSIM, which needs no vocabulary harmonisation, so all sixteen annotations enter on their own terms. On the NSCLC cohort, pathological response separates patients under fourteen of the sixteen. The strength is ordered by reference rather than by algorithm: holding the algorithm fixed, the three references differ several-fold in how strongly patients separate, and the weakest is not significant. The separations are small throughout, so composition carries a detectable shift rather than a partition.
Where that variance sits also differs. Taking the cell types needed to reach half the compositional variance, ProjecTILs needs three and Chu four, and each includes its own progenitor label; huARdb needs six, all of them coarse exhausted or effector classes, and places both of its progenitor poles near the bottom of its eighteen. A label that is near-absent cannot vary between patients.


Swapping the annotation loses a published clinical result
A published biomarker from an NSCLC anti-PD1 cohort predicts recurrence-free survival. Its construction is clonal, not phenotypic: it measures how far a patient’s tumor-reactive clonal compartment has progressed toward terminal exhaustion. Holding that construction fixed and swapping only the annotation, no reference’s transcriptomic Tpex label reconstitutes it: all four are unestimable as predictors, because a reference’s Tpex label is close to absent from the clonally Tex-related compartment. Decision-curve analysis puts two of them below treating nobody at most treatment thresholds between 15% and 45%.
Tested for differential abundance instead, state by state and then across huARdb’s published hierarchy, the answer does not change. Five of six definitions show no credible association with response; the one that does is NR-enriched, pointing away from a progenitor biomarker. Nothing aggregates to a coarse exhausted class as a whole, and the single node whose interval excludes zero is an interferon-stimulated label depleted in responders.
This is not evidence that Tpex frequency fails to predict outcome. On the same cells under a progenitor-to-terminal ratio every estimate points the same way, with all hazard ratios below 1, but only the clonal construction reaches significance. No reference’s transcriptomic Tpex label does. Several constructions on one set of cells give several different answers.


What the references do agree on
Measured on the reference atlases themselves, none of the three progenitor poles is depleted from lymph node. Relative to how much lymph node each atlas contains, Chu’s p-Tex is 5.1 times enriched there, huARdb’s Tex-Tpex 1.8 times and its SELL+ pole 1.1 times, rising to 2.3 when the comparison is restricted to the solid-tumor stratum. That is computed on the 1,125,712 and 110,218 cells of those two references with no annotation transfer involved, so it cannot inherit the circularity that affects comparisons made on annotated query cohorts.
The same direction appears in patients who contributed both a lymph node and a paired tumor, where the progenitor-to-terminal ratio is higher in the node. That version rests on 2 to 8 paired patients per cohort with substantial heterogeneity and one arm reversing, and most of those cohorts are reference training data, so it is reported as corroboration rather than as the primary evidence.
A coarse biological gradient therefore survives annotation choice even where cell-level identity does not, which bounds the scope of the disagreement reported above.

title: Tpex Data Portal
text:
Caveats

No ground truth. Every comparison is annotation against annotation. Nothing here identifies a correct tool.
Definitional, not calibration. The references disagree because they encode different cuts of one continuous trajectory, not because one is fitted badly. Each has been useful in prior work.
Training overlap is flagged, not hidden. Headline numbers use held-out combinations only.
Compartment results are descriptive. They show the level differs between lymph node and tumor; they do not show that a nodal ratio predicts outcome.
Projection mode is not uniform. Anchor-based projection does not complete against the 1,125,712-cell huARdb atlas, so that reference’s ProjecTILs arm uses direct projection while the other fifteen pipelines are anchored.
Clinical verdicts are sensitive to which annotation is used. Swapping the annotation moves several results, including one that reaches significance under some annotations and not others. Direction is stable; significance and credibility are not. Individual verdicts should not be read alone.
One reference names a lymphoid population. huARdb’s SELL+ Tpex sits in lymph node and blood and is near-absent from tumor, so in a tumor-only cohort most patients carry none of it. Its progenitor-to-terminal ratio is not reported for that reason.
huARdb’s infection content lands on one pole, not the atlas as a whole. The atlas draws 25.3% of its cells from infection and its SELL+ Tpex pole 27.6%, so the raw fractions barely separate. Holding the compartment fixed at blood is what shows the localisation: there it is Tex-Tpex that is infection-enriched and depleted in the blood of patients with cancer, while the SELL+ pole is not. The worry therefore attaches to the pole we treat as tumor-leaning, which is the opposite of what the atlas’s overall composition suggests.

title: Tpex Data Portal
text:
Navigation
The figures page carries each plate with its claim. The source and analysis code are held in a repository that will be released with publication, and every table and figure is reproducible from it. The manuscript carries every algorithm-by-reference comparison, statistic and caveat in full.

The schema marks input.cohort as nullable, but leave it set unless there is a reason not to. It drives the reference source-overlap audit, and in the contract’s own words “an undeclared cohort means the audit cannot be performed.” That audit matters here more than it might elsewhere: the three references are not independent sources, so a discordance number computed without knowing which cohort produced it is hard to interpret.

Code
matrix_source = matrix_kind === "X" ? ".X" : `layers.${layer_name.trim()}`







The matrix selector is always written out in full and is never inferred, because the upload validator refuses to guess: it detects a transposed matrix or non-integer values and reports them rather than fixing them. The contract’s reason for that is worth repeating, since it is the same failure this whole project is about: auto-transpose and auto-normalize are forbidden because they “would silently fabricate Tpex calls.”

scratch and output are relative per-run names, not full paths. The installation supplies the roots and appends this value literally, which is why gse243013-standard is right and results/gse243013-standard double-nests when the configured output root already ends in results. Memory should be sized for peak R-side usage, not just the Python orchestrator; the reference mapping is the expensive half.






This form never writes a scheduler, an account, a partition, a queue, a reference location, or a filesystem root. Those are owned by the cluster installation, not by the analysis. That separation is what lets the same analysis.yaml move between institutions unchanged.

title: Build an analysis
Build an analysis
text:
5. Running it on the cluster


Code
html`<pre><code>${[
  `# 1. check the file and the input against the contract. No compute.`,
  `tpex validate ${name.trim() || "analysis"}.yaml`,
  ``,
  `# 2. resolve the immutable plan and preview what would run.`,
  `tpex plan     ${name.trim() || "analysis"}.yaml`,
  ``,
  `# 3. materialize the workflow and submit it to the scheduler.`,
  `tpex run      ${name.trim() || "analysis"}.yaml`
].join("\n")}</code></pre>`







tpex run resolves the plan and validates the input first; it stops there as a read-only preview unless it is submitted explicitly, so it is safe to try. When the run finishes the user will have tpex_result_<run_id>.zip, which tpex results verify will check and which the bundle viewer reads.






tpex install and the no-argument tpex are not yet implemented. Until they land, the file this page writes is still correct and still validates, but an installation configured another way is needed for the roots it deliberately leaves out.

title: Reference atlases
text:
Every annotation in this study is a label transferred from one of these three atlases. They are not independent of each other: all three include Yost 2019 (GSE123813) among their source studies, which is disclosed rather than corrected for. Each names at least one progenitor-exhausted state, and huARdb names two of its own, so there are four poles in total across three atlases.
Findings are preliminary, and human tumors carry no ground-truth Tpex label, so these pages describe where each atlas draws its boundary rather than which one is right.


Code
idx = FileAttachment("atlas-data/index.json").json()
Inputs.table(idx, {
  columns: ["atlas", "cells", "states", "poles"],
  header: {atlas: "atlas", cells: "cells", states: "annotated states",
           poles: "progenitor label(s)"},
  width: {atlas: 190}
})

















CD8 TILs: Built entirely from tumor and metastasis tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, with no lymph node or blood, so its progenitor pole is a tumor-resident, Tex-bridged one.
huARdb v2: A 1,125,712-cell pan-tissue atlas, 65.4% of it peripheral blood and 25.3% from infection rather than cancer. That infection content is not spread evenly: within blood it is the Tex-Tpex pole that is infection-enriched (Ro/e 2.07) and depleted in cancer blood (0.23), while SELL+ Tpex is not (0.89). It is the only one of the three that names two progenitor poles of its own, and the only one publishing a cell-type hierarchy.
Chu pan-cancer: A pan-cancer T-cell atlas. Like CD8 TILs it is tumor-built, and the two are still near-disjoint on which cells they call progenitor.
